#1091. Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dyani Lewis is a freelance journalist in Melbourne, Australia.

In August 1987, a scandal erupted over work on the world’s highest mountain range. John Talent, a palaeontologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, announced he had found numerous anomalies in research charting the geology of the Himalayas. All of the problems were in papers by Vishwa Jit Gupta, one of India’s most celebrated palaeontologists at the time.

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

More than 10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023 — a new record

Gupta was outraged. But further investigations over the following seven years revealed the scale and brazenness of his fraud. Littered through more than 450 publications were maps of collection sites that didn’t exist, plagiarized images and specimens stolen from collections that Gupta had visited. More than 100 experts had been duped into co-authoring descriptions of fossils Gupta claimed he had collected from specific Himalayan geological formations, but instead hailed from North America and Morocco.

“It destroyed the image of Indian science,” says retired geologist Ghulam Bhat, who completed his PhD on Himalayan geology in the same year that the allegations of fraud emerged.

Gupta died in 2022, and many geologists know to steer clear of his work. But awareness of the problem is fading, and none of Gupta’s papers have been retracted. When Nature contacted Bhat, who is now editor-in-chief of the Journal of the Geological Society of India (JGSI), he was unaware that Gupta’s papers were not marked as retracted. That’s despite the JGSI’s 1991 evaluation of 19 of Gupta’s papers that it published1, which concluded that “the fossil finds of V. J. Gupta are not reliable [...] the data is incomplete bordering on disinformation”.

Much of Gupta’s work is inaccessible, having been published in now-defunct periodicals or in volumes that, although digitized online, have not been indexed in reference bibliometric databases such as Scopus, Web of Science and Dimensions. Despite this, Gupta’s falsehoods are now being propagated outside specialist circles, as his old journal articles are being surfaced through artificial-intelligence tools that summarize search results. When someone searches for geological landmarks in the Himalayas, such as the Tandi Limestone, Google’s AI overview obliges with direct links to Gupta’s discredited papers.

Bhat now plans to rectify the digital record and says that all other journals that have published Gupta’s work should do the same. “If this problem is left as it is, unattended, it will pollute all of the geological literature in future,” he says. Gupta also published papers in Nature in the 1960s; Chris Graf, director of research integrity at Springer Nature, didn’t confirm that the journal would re-examine them. But he added that in general, when investigations of old papers are hampered by limited available information, an editorial expression of concern “is likely to be our preferred mechanism for alerting readers to potential issues”. (Nature’s news team is editorially independent of its publisher, Springer Nature.)

The Himalayas case raises a wider issue: how to deal with fraudulent, unethical or even merely incorrect research from decades ago, especially in an era in which much old work is digitized and AI systems can pick up studies that might previously have been neglected.

There are many skeletons in science’s closet, but publishers can be reluctant to judge science of the past by today’s standards, and can find it more difficult to issue retractions when authors are dead, original records cannot be consulted or journals are no longer in print.

And as publishers struggle to deal with the fallout from rising research fraud and AI slop, finite resources can also mean that many old papers with known flaws are left as they are.

Gráinne McNamara, a council member of the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) in Eastleigh, UK, which advises journals on best practice, says that journals are increasingly contacting COPE to ask for advice about dealing with concerns on very old papers.

“Everybody is looking for what’s the best, most responsible way to handle these,” she says.

The widespread use of retractions as a mechanism for maintaining integrity in the scientific record is a relatively recent phenomenon. The JGSI evaluation report about Gupta served as a warning notice to the community at the time, but didn’t use the word retraction. It also pre-dates the modern standardization of retraction processes, which happened in the 2000s. Now, a journal should issue a retraction notice, and leave the original paper intact, but with a modified title and a stamp or watermark indicating that it has been retracted. The information should then feed through to bibliographic databases.

In the early 2000s, only around 30 retraction notices were published each year, and COPE first developed guidelines to standardize the retraction process in 2004. The number — and rate — of retractions has exploded since then, with more than 10,000 recorded in 2023 alone.

Digitization of old records, combined with a wider propensity to retract flawed work, has seen journals reaching farther back in time to retract studies — and this has led to some startlingly long gaps between when an article was published and when it was formally retracted. Retraction Watch, an initiative that curates a database of more than 70,000 retractions and expressions of concern (a notice that highlights potential issues with a publication), has reported that the longest gap is 80 years. That’s for a prank case report published in 1923 in the Dutch medical journal Nederlands Tijdschrift voor Geneeskunde.

It described a man who died from “piss cough”, an affliction that caused him to cough up liquid smelling of urine. In 2003, an editor at the journal happened to look up the case, which he thought was widely known to be a hoax. Realizing it had never been retracted and that others did not know it was fake, he sought confirmation of the hoax, and found it in the autobiography of a retired University of Amsterdam physician, who had helped to cook up the nonsense case when he was a medical student. Accompanying commentary on the journal’s website said that a retraction was appropriate now that the older literature had become accessible through digitization.

According to Nature’s analysis of Retraction Watch data — which capture a subset of total retractions — the number of old papers that are being retracted is rising. Overall, some 358 retraction notices and 120 expressions of concern have been issued for papers or book chapters that were more than 20 years old at the time of the editorial action (see ‘Retracting the past’). This is still a rare phenomenon: since 2015, the oldest retractions represent some 0.7% of the total number, up from 0.2% before 2010. But around 3% of expressions of concern have occurred for works older than 20 years. That illustrates how publishers might choose to issue expressions of concern for older papers, rather than retract, because it can be harder to investigate historical records.

In 2005, biochemist Barry Milborrow sought to retract five of his own papers, published between 1980 and 1982, on biochemical pathways that bacteria, algae and plants use to make pigments, because later work had disproved their findings. The Biochemical Journal, which published Milborrow’s self-retraction listing the five articles2, retracted both articles it had published. Another journal issued a correction, but no notice was issued by the publisher of the remaining two papers. Ian Swift, Milborrow’s co-author and PhD student at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, at the time, says he only found out about the retractions many years later, after Milborrow had passed away.

According to COPE guidance, journal editors can retract articles if they no longer have confidence in the results and conclusions reported in them. By that rubric, many older papers could, in theory, be retracted, but, being rarely cited, are usually left alone.

Even when invalid papers are still being cited, retraction might not follow. In 1985, for instance, geneticist Svante Pääbo reported that he had cloned DNA from an Egyptian mummy3. The seminal work marked the birth of palaeogenomics, a field that earned Pääbo a Nobel prize in 2022. But the mummy DNA was actually contamination from a modern handler, as Pääbo, now at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, has openly acknowledged. “What is problematic is if false conclusions lead other scientists and the community as a whole astray,” he told Nature when asked for this article. “I don’t think anyone is currently misled by the mummy paper,” he says, which is why he argues that the work should stand, adding that to correct very old papers with errors “would create more confusion than clarity”.

Retractions can reshape scientists’ careers in unexpected ways

Retractions can reshape scientists’ careers in unexpected ways

In practice, old papers tend to be considered for retraction only if they have widespread integrity issues that journal editors feel shouldn’t be allowed to stand unmarked. A major trigger for mass retractions of older work is when investigations of an individual’s research cast doubt over their entire body of work. For instance, a 2019 investigation by King’s College London into the work of psychologist Hans Eysenck and his German collaborator Ronald Grossarth-Maticek has led to papers dating back to the 1940s being flagged — albeit many with expressions of concern rather than retractions.

Eysenck died in 1997 as one of the most celebrated psychologists of the twentieth century. But in 2019, psychiatrist Anthony Pelosi, who had critiqued Eysenck’s work to no effect in the 1990s, published a renewed analysis of the studies4. An accompanying editorial called on King’s College London — where Eysenck worked from 1955 until 1983 — to conduct a formal investigation. The investigation report, also published in 2019, concluded that 24 articles by Eysenck and Maticek published between 1988 and 2000 were ‘unsafe’ and recommended they be retracted.

Those recommendations weren’t followed entirely. Only 16 of the 24 papers have been retracted, and another 4 have expressions of concern. Four remain unflagged. After sustained criticism over the narrow scope of the 2019 investigation, King’s College London published a statement in October 2025 saying that other publications based on the data set used in the 24 papers it examined are also likely to be ‘unsafe’ and should be flagged by journal editors — although it did not list affected publications.

So far, 94 of Eysenck’s hundreds of papers have been either retracted or tagged with an expression of concern, the oldest of which was published in 1943 (see ‘Longest gaps’).

Such inconsistencies in how publishers deal with research-integrity issues are common and don’t relate only to very old papers, says Andrew Grey, an endocrinologist and research-integrity specialist at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. He alerted publishers to concerns over large numbers of articles by Yoshihiro Sato, a Japanese bone-health researcher who fabricated data in dozens of clinical trials, and has reported seeing some journals respond with retractions or expressions of concern, whereas others take no action5.

One famous scandal of the past — the 1980s discrediting of work by John Darsee, a US biologist — has led to just 17 retractions. Although news reports at the time stated that more than 80 of Darsee’s papers had been retracted, this refers to editorial notes and warnings that, in parallel with the Gupta case, don’t appear in modern records as retractions.

Another trigger for retracting old work is when it attracts renewed attention, particularly in medical fields.

Each year, Marcel van der Heyden, a physiologist at the University Medical Center Utrecht in the Netherlands, asks his final-year students to write a review article about a poison or toxin. In 2025, he chose caesium salts, and his students uncovered 20 case reports of people ingesting the toxic chemical6. Often, the individuals deliberately consumed the compound as an alternative treatment for cancer. Although the US Food and Drug Administration cautioned against its use in 2018, the deadly ‘therapy’ is still promoted in books and online by some wellness centres.

The treatment traces back to two papers published in 1984 in Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior. One of the papers was written by Austrian-born Hellfried Sartori, who had been prosecuted in Maryland in 1982 for fraud relating to using the unproven cancer treatment. That case ended in a mistrial. Sartori subsequently had his medical licence revoked in several US states in the 1980s and was sentenced to prison in Virginia in 1999 for practising medicine without a licence. And in 2010, an inquest into the deaths of five people in Australia found that he had been treating patients remotely from Thailand. Many more of his patients had also died under his treatment, the court heard.

The other paper promoting caesium therapy was by Wisconsin-based Aubrey Keith Brewer. Brewer died in 1986, but his namesake Brewer International Science Library continues to distribute information on caesium and other alternative therapies with a disclaimer that the protocols are “for information purposes only”, and that people should consult their physician if unwell. Nature contacted the website but received no response.

Van der Heyden contacted Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior in August 2025, suggesting an expression of concern could be warranted. “Without the original data, it’s hard to tell whether there is a mistake made, or whether it’s on purpose,” he says. But the research-integrity team at the journal’s publisher, Elsevier, decided in January this year to remove the two papers, soon after Van der Heyden informed them that his review had been accepted for publication and that his university was poised to issue a press release about it. The papers were deleted entirely this April, as Retraction Watch reported.

The move to scrub a paper, rather than merely retract and leave it in place, can be taken if the contents could present a serious health risk to the public, according to COPE guidelines.

#1090. USMNT cancel media access as Man United eye Mauricio Pochettino swoop

Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as the clear frontrunner to be the next Manchester United manager

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Media duties scheduled for Wednesday have been cancelled by the United States as Manchester United prepare to make a move for their head coach Mauricio Pochettino.

It is understood that plans are underway at United to appoint the Argentinian should current head coach Michael Carrick, as expected, be dismissed, with the club currently sitting in the relegation zone after their worst start to a season since 1986.

Pochettino is understood to be keen on the Old Trafford post, having previously been linked with the vacancy on prior occasions when it became available.

US Soccer confirmed that planned player media access on Wednesday was called off in observance of Veterans Day, removing any opportunity for Pochettino’s squad to be asked about reports regarding his prospective departure.

The former Tottenham, Paris St Germain and Chelsea boss signed a contract extension to stay on as USMNT head coach until the 2030 World Cup only three months ago, meaning US Soccer would be owed compensation if he agrees to join United.

Despite the growing uncertainty surrounding his future, the Englishman arrived for training as normal at United’s Carrington complex on Wednesday morning.

He left Carrington on Wednesday afternoon with no announcement on his future having been made. Carrick’s position was discussed by chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox in a meeting in Monaco with United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe on Wednesday.

A 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como and a 3-0 loss at home to Bournemouth had left Carrick’s position under severe threat, but the board chose to grant him the opportunity to turn things around.

Carrick’s side subsequently suffered a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea, where they failed to take their chances and had Lisandro Martinez sent off, prior to last Tuesday’s thrilling 3-2 Champions League comeback win over Roma.

An extraordinary 4-4 draw against Aston Villa followed on Sunday, after which the head coach maintained he would not resign and was planning for the international break as usual.

"I’m pretty clear where we need to go and how we need to get there," Carrick said.

"Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so.

"But as a normal international week is, you know, we’ll have some training. We’ll have one or two days off, but not too much. But we’ll train, and we’ll get ready for the next game."

United return to action with a Premier League trip to rivals Liverpool on November 22, a fixture they could enter with Pochettino in the dugout.

Pochettino has spoken with United regarding the post several times over the years, including in 2022 when the club chose to hire Erik ten Hag instead.

There is deep mutual respect between Pochettino and former United manager Sir Alex Ferguson. The pair have met on numerous occasions, with Ferguson known to have been greatly impressed by his Southampton team in 2013.

Pochettino has also spoken about watching the 1999 Champions League final in Barcelona, where Ferguson’s United side sealed the treble.

#1089. Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

The big talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

“After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” said Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

It was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

“I need to praise the players,” said Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”

When it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” said Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

One last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down quickly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

Arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

This is about as dominant as Newcastle have been in a game all season but they have not been able to find a goal from some where. They have just gone close again as Will Osula just fails to reach Amar Dedic’s cross.

Arteta has made another double sub: Hincapie and Eze replace Tzolis and Calafiori, so all change down the left flank. For Hull, Lucas Herrington has replaced the injured Semi Ajayi at the back.

Felt like the cheers for Viktor Gyokeres to replace Kai Havertz were as much a reflection on frustrations with the German as enthusiasm for the Swede. Havertz has struggled today and is far less convincing in this sort of match – when the onus is more on the Arsenal to create – than he was in scoring the winner at Anfield last Sunday.

Specific explanation for Declan Rice’s substitution is unclear – he didn’t look injured – and so perhaps just reflection of risks associated with a third 90 minutes in six days alongside an acknowledgement of quality alternatives on the bench.

Some changes at the Emirates: Cho and Lewie Coyle are replaced by Joe Gelhardt and Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

It has been all Newcastle at the start of the second half and Harvey Barnes has now failed to take a hat-trick of chances. This was the best of the lot, running on to the ball, middle of the area from a perfectly weighted Yoane Wissa pass, he blasted a shot the wrong side of the post.

The second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

While Kai Havertz was in an offside position when his shirt was pulled, he may not have been active.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

However, the Premier League match centre does not see it that way.

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Frustrating first half for Arsenal, but it was never going to be easy to go again in the Premier League following a Champions League away game and last Sunday’s big win against Liverpool. Hull have also played with confidence and resolve.

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

I’ve spotted something else since I was covering Arsenal in 2018. I was gazing up at the boards that circle the top tier where the club mark every trophy that the team has won. There was previously this big gap, of course, from 2005 until 2014 before the cabinet gradually began refilling. But someone has since had a good idea. They have added all the women’s trophies as well, transforming the tally by just the odd 17 during those tricky years of transition and billionaire rivals owners in the men’s game.

Declan Rice has also just had a shot flash wide, but still no clear chances for either team.

Dan Burn thought he had scored from close-range, but Wissa has been penalised for blocking Castagne so the goal was ruled out.

#FULNEW – 33' The referee's call of no goal to Newcastle United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Wissa fouled Castagne in the build-up. AR2: "Defensive foul at the back post. Wissa holding at the back post". REF: "Castagne held back by Wissa. It's a deliberate foul". VAR: "He's clearly holding him - confirming the on-field decision of defensive free-kick. Wissa is clearly making an attempt to hold the Fulham defender. Clear holding offence".

Some controversy here as Newcastle appear to have had a perfectly good goal ruled out for an innocuous looking foul from Yoane Wissa on Timothy Costagne inside the box. Dan Burn was the scorer. Newcastle’s bench are furious. Most of us are just bemused.

Arsenal have largely been on top after Hull’s lively start but clear chances are scarce and Hull’s fans certainly sound increasingly confident. “You’re only here for the Tigers”, they say. To which a rendition of “champions” rings out. On that note, they had a replica of the Premier League trophy outside the Emirates before the match, with fans queuing up to get their photo with it.

The bright start from the visitors has not been maintained and Fulham have been on top for the last few minutes. Lukasz Hornicek just made a full-stretch save to deny Oscar Bobb and there is a sense inside the stadium that the first goal is coming.

Newcastle, as we have seen all too often recently, really struggle to pass through the lines and when the ball makes it out wide it invariably seems to go backwards again.

Although Harvey Barnes has just forced a good save from Leno from a Jacob Murphy cross. It was easily Newcastle’s best move of the match as Wissa and Osula linked up for the first time through the middle.

David Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Kai Havertz was going away from goal but Nobel Medy hardly subtle with his challenge – arm and leg – on the edge of the area. It would have been what we call soft but the sort of innocuous challenge that very often results in a foul elsewhere on the pitch.

On a self-indulgent note, this is an all-too-rare trip to the Emirates for me. I covered Arsenal for the last decade of the Arsene Wenger era, ending in 2018 and haven’t made many visits since. A few things are already striking: so many familiar faces still among the staff at a club that has always had more of a family feel than most. Outside, and few of the gaps in the middle (or top tier) that became evident during the final Wenger years when many fans clearly lost faith in the team’s title-winning credentials. The atmosphere is a notch up too.

Thiaw heads wide after a well-worked short corner from Newcastle, but the flag is up for offside in any case. Lewis Hall with the cross.

A decent start from Newcastle United against Fulham and you can see clearer patterns of play emerging. The fact that Fulham are constantly looking to build their attacks by playing out from the back has also helped. The home side have had a couple of scares already.

Hull gain some territory in the early exchanges, and win a corner via a long throw. From the set-piece, Egan’s set-piece hit the side-netting. A shot across Arsenal’s bows.

The lack of Mohamed Beloloumi’s creative spark clearly a big blow for Hull against the best defence in the league; a defence that will be further strengthened by the imminent return of William Saliba. Mikel Arteta had decided that Saliba would be better served by playing against Aston Villa for the Under-21s at Boreham Wood tomorrow. Hull have started on the front, though, in the opening minutes

Updates to follow from the Emirates and Craven Cottage. The Last Post was played and there was a minute’s silence as both grounds mark Remembrance Day.

It’s always great to be back home. It’s the last game before the international break so we know the importance of that and the challenges Hull will provide today. We’re super focused, it’s a massive game for us.

With the amount of games we’re playing, we need that freshness. The team has been performing really well, the finishers have been key again and that’s what we have today – start the game really, really strong and if we need to, have the ability to change the game.

Arsenal’s manager says the centre-back will play an Under-21s game tomorrow as the continues his recovery from a back injury.

Arteta says: “In regards to Willy as well, he needs some minutes. Obviously, the Champions League allows you to bring more players into the bench, but we believe that it’s the best thing to do: to play some minutes at the weekend with the Under-21s and then be fully fit for the international break.”

Arsenal are playing very good football, no matter Champions League or Premier League. They are very strong, they control everything not just against us, also other better clubs. But in football, we have a chance. Obviously, they are a big favourite, and we can start to try to create some difficulties for them.

The return of Sean Steur is a positive move from Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle but is it also a sign the German is feeling the pressure of public opinion on Tyneside?

The 18-year-old has looked the best of Newcastle’s summer signings but Newcastle are understandably trying to ease the teenager into things.

Ultimately, though, Steur is the only midfield player who can take possession of the ball under pressure and despite his tender years they have looked a better side with him in it.

There have been widespread calls for Steur to be called back into the side and Jaissle has done just that for a game he could really do with winning coming off the back of four defeats in their last five games.

Malick Thiaw also comes back into the side for Fabian Schar, with Jacob Murphy preferred to Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa starting in place of Joe Willock. I don’t think any of those dropped can have any complaints.

However, the constant chopping and changing betrays the problems Jaissle is facing. Whatever team he sends out is struggling to deliver what he wants, both individually and collectively.

With the international break coming up, Newcastle need a positive result to quieten the negative noise.

Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal are “looking after” Declan Rice more now than in any previous campaign and has rejected suggestions that the England midfielder is being overplayed.

Rice played through nerve pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season, when he made an extraordinary 69 appearances for club and country.

The 27-year-old has played at least 60 matches in each of the past four campaigns, prompting concerns among Arsenal supporters that he is at risk of burnout or injury.

Arteta kept Rice on the field for the full 90 minutes of Arsenal’s midweek victory over Slavia Prague but insisted the club is working harder than ever to manage the midfielder’s workload.

So far this season, Rice has been left out of Arsenal’s two Carabao Cup matches and also withdrew from the previous international break in September.

Asked if he was concerned about Rice’s fitness, Arteta said: “Concerns? Which is the only player, the only player in this squad, that for two games in the Carabao Cup has been left out of the squad? At home with two days off? It’s not true [that Rice is being overplayed].

“We are really looking after him more than any other season. The way he is training and all the love [he is being shown]. That’s it.

“Here are the demands of this football club and a player like him. Not only him, because there are many others that have even less time. That’s it. That has to be the mindset. If you start to put other things in your brain, [it will create] damage. Erase them, get them in the bin and just focus on what you have to do.”

Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.

#1088. Man United face final hurdle to close deal for Mauricio Pochettino as new manager

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Argentine coach is the front-runner to replace Michael Carrick at Old Trafford, with the club inside the relegation zone during the international break

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester United are closing in on a deal to appoint Mauricio Pochettino before their next game against Liverpool with Michael Carrick set to be sacked.

United must strike a deal with US Soccer, with a solution required over the United States’ next two international games in particular, while the club’s hierarchy is meeting at a Monaco summit to finalise a decision over the club’s manager.

Compensation, worth an initial $7m (£5.3m), will be a formality due to the clause in Pochettino’s existing contract, that runs until the 2030 World Cup.

While additional compensation will be required for Pochettino’s trusted coaching staff, including long-time assistant Jesus Perez.

The United States face Concacaf Nations League fixtures against Haiti during the current international break, with an away match on 14 November and a home match in Cincinnati on 18 November.

US Soccer are currently planning for Pochettino to be in charge of both games, though United will push to have Pochettino available sooner, with their next Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

Another option is potentially for Darren Fletcher to be handed an interim role once more, should a deal be unable to conclude in time.

While losing Pochettino would be a blow for the USA, The Independent understands that US Soccer has been prepared for the prospect of his exit at some stage before the 2030 World Cup, with a succession plan already in place.

Pochettino’s move back to England would be a major shift in his plans after committing to a four-year build to the 2030 World Cup, having overseen an encouraging, yet ultimately unsuccessful home World Cup this summer, ending in a heavy defeat to Belgium in the last 16.

While Pochettino admitted in September that he was “excited” for the journey to Spain, Portugal and Morocco, he conceded four years is a “long time” and that this commitment was “different”.

"We are serious people,” Pochettino told The Independent and other outlets in a wide-ranging interview. “Now it's a different thing. When we gave our word to the federation, it was about starting and finishing, after the World Cup. It's different, maybe, if you ask me now. Because now we commit to four years.

“Always it's different. Before, it was very easy to say 'OK, we start now, we prepare the team for the World Cup, we play the World Cup, and then we'll see.' [Leaving] before that, it was difficult. Because we committed before. For us, it was the moment to say 'if some club came, it's impossible'. Now it's another question.

“For us it was impossible to think about coming back, or going to another club. Because we received some calls from different clubs. But we cannot go away, first, because we didn't want to go. Always you can break a contract, say you stop, and that's it, you agree something. But in the moment I think it wasn't right for us to create all these situations and expectations.

"And now it's a four year contract, it's different. We can next season lose the Copa America or the Gold Cup, and they're not happy with us, they can sack us, or we can say, 'ok it's not in the way that we think'. Four years is different. Maybe now if someone calls in the future, it's a different, different type. We are excited, we are thinking to spend four years, I think to the next World Cup. But now it's a long period."

#1087. Scottish defender makes comeback after seven-year absence from national team

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The defender has impressed since moving to Turkey this summer, earning a chance to add to his four international caps as Scotland prepare for a crucial double-header.

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

David Bates has been recalled to the Scotland squad almost eight years after his last appearance, following a strong opening spell in Turkey.

The 30-year-old centre-back joins Sebastien Pocognoli’s squad after Luis Binks withdrew ahead of Nations League matches against North Macedonia on Friday and Switzerland on Monday.

Bates has started all 11 games for Amedspor this term as they have risen to third in the Turkish Super Lig.

The defender won his four caps under Alex McLeish while at Hamburg in 2018/19. His last outing was a 2-0 Euro 2020 qualifying win over San Marino in March 2019, McLeish’s final fixture in charge.

Former Rangers player Bates joined Amedspor this summer after four years in Belgium with Mechelen and Standard Liege following his 2022 Aberdeen departure.

Brondby captain Binks is the second centre-back to exit Pocognoli’s squad, after Swansea’s Stephen Welsh suffered an injury and was replaced by Los Angeles FC’s Ryan Porteous last weekend.

The head coach sees the double-header as vital to preparing for Euro 2028 qualification, which may start in March if Scotland avoid Nations League play-offs.

"I think that these two games are, if we start the qualification in March, the last package of games that we have to use to be ready for the March camp," Pocognoli said.

"If it’s not the case (that the Euro campaign starts in March), we can play friendly games which can be useful for June, so we have more time to prepare. And maybe, if we are really strong in the next two games, maybe we have play-off games. That’s the ambition.

"These can be useful also for the process of the qualification. But if the qualification starts (in March), we need to be ready. That’s why this camp for me is crucial in terms of demanding to the players, try to impress me and do everything to improve.

"I believe if we want to go to the Euros and be successful, we need to build this qualification feeling by winning games and to build the best winning culture possible."

Michael Carrick is expected to be sacked, but Manchester United are yet to make an official announcement after days of speculation

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Peter Schmeichel has accused Manchester United of "disrespectful" treatment towards Michael Carrick as rumours linking Mauricio Pochettino to the club persist.

It is understood that plans are already arranged to bring in the Argentinian if head coach Carrick is removed from his post as expected.

Pochettino, currently coaching the United States national side, is believed to be open to taking over at Old Trafford.

Former United keeper Schmeichel believes the root problems lie above Carrick, arguing the head coach should be allowed to sign players in the January window.

"I absolutely do feel sympathy for him. I think the way this is playing out is very disrespectful to him," Schmeichel told The Overlap Daily.

"If I’m honest, I don’t think he’s doing anything wrong. I know the team that he’s in charge of is where they are in the table, but I don’t put all of that on him.

"There are so many things that have been going on at Manchester United literally since Sir Alex (Ferguson) and David Gill left the club. And it’s never been corrected. It’s not been the correct people, not the right people in charge, and slowly it’s just gone worse.

"And if you think about this transfer window now, it’s abundantly clear to everyone – everyone who knows just a little bit about football – that Manchester United needed defenders.

"They got through a whole transfer window without signing a single defender. You can’t win games if you concede 30 goals in 10 games…that was not addressed.

"So yes, I do feel a lot of sympathy for Michael. I think what is happening is wrong. I think we should stick with Michael.

"I think we should just try and steady the ship a little bit and then get into January and then sign the players that he feels he needs to bring the team forward and then be realistic about what this season is all about."

Pochettino earned acclaim during his tenure at Tottenham, taking them to the 2019 Champions League final. Former striker Harry Kane praised his former boss on Wednesday, reflecting on their time together.

"Me and Mauricio obviously have a fantastic relationship," he said. "I mentioned him as one of the coaches who had a big impact on my career and definitely my development at that stage in my career.

"I needed his guidance. The way he pushed me, not just on the pitch but off the pitch as well was really, really helpful.

"Obviously a fantastic coach, he’s managed the biggest clubs in the world. From my point of view, I can’t speak highly enough of him. We’ll have to wait and see what happens but I know he’s a great guy and also a fantastic manager."

#1084. Harry Kane: ‘My biggest fear is finishing my career thinking I could have done more’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Interview: The England captain discusses his elite mentality and the long journey from debut nerves to a historic 126th cap when he surpasses Peter Shilton’s record at Wembley on Thursday night

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Harry Kane has answered every critic and extinguished every doubt. At 33 he is a double winner with Bayern Munich, England’s greatest goalscorer, and sits on the Ballon d’Or throne. On Thursday night, Kane will reach another famous milestone when he surpasses Peter Shilton’s tally of England caps and collects his 126th against Croatia in the Nations League at Wembley.

From the academy coaches at Arsenal who released him aged eight, to the Tottenham coaches who didn’t think he could handle first-team football, to the fans who labelled him a one-season wonder and the pundits who prematurely called time on his England career, each served to motivate Kane. You might think he would finally feel satisfied, vindicated, ready to drop his guard, to take his foot off the pedal, to eat a Twix or two.

Far from it. Kane is speaking to a huddle of journalists at Tottenham’s training ground, back where his career began, and insists he still has a point to prove.

“I don’t think that will ever leave me,” he says. “It’s probably part of what makes me push myself to the limits because in football, you’ve never completed it. No matter what you’ve achieved, there is always a trophy that someone else has won or a goal record that someone else has. There’s always something. Whether it’s noise from the outside, media or the fans or whatever it may be, it just helps motivate me to realise there’s a lot more to achieve.”

Where does that come from? How can the unassuming man who stood on stage at the London Palladium last month, nervously twiddling his buttons and repeatedly sweeping away specks of nothing from his pristine tuxedo, who spent his 12-minute speech naming dozens of people who had helped his career, also be a ferociously driven world-class athlete who carries a kind of burning wrath inside him?

“I think it’s just my mindset, because I’ve had to prove people wrong my whole career. From early academy days proving coaches wrong, proving scouts wrong, it has just been instilled in me. If someone tells me I can’t do something it just motivates me more to do it. Of course, you have to combine the mentality with being able to produce it, so that’s where the self-belief and the training and all the consistent work I do has allowed me to do that.

“I’ve spoken about Tom Brady before and that unwavering mentality to be the best. Maybe with me, because I’m a calm person, you don’t see the ego of some of these great players and I’m a bit more relaxed, but it doesn’t mean that I don’t want it as much as everyone else. It doesn’t mean I don’t put in the work and drive myself and drive everyone around me to be the best.

“Maybe getting released that early and proving them wrong and then maybe proving my early coaches at Tottenham [wrong], just bit by bit, loan moves that didn’t go quite well, again, same thing – ‘I’m going to show them’ – using all the negative stuff as motivation to push me to another level.”

There is something else behind Kane’s drive, a different kind of emotion: the dread of leaving a single stone unturned.

“My biggest fear is finishing my career and thinking I could have done a bit more if I could have just done that or done that. I want to make sure that I cross every bridge so that whenever that day does come, I can say I’ve done everything possible, I have this record, I don’t have this record – but it doesn’t matter, I can sleep well at night.”

Kane can still remember arriving at his first England camp, in the spring of 2015, and admits he felt “nervous and anxious” about being the new guy. Wayne Rooney was the England captain and was the first person to talk to the 21-year-old Spurs striker. “He told me to just be myself,” Kane says.

But as soon as he got on the training pitch, Kane felt a confidence flood through his body. “I felt like this is my comfort zone, I know what I can do, I can score goals, I can even talk and shout – I felt more comfortable in that sense. I remember training really well and feeling like, ‘OK, if I can do it here I can do it anywhere’, and that gave me even more confidence. I just took that into the game.”

Kane replaced Rooney in the second half and scored 79 seconds later with his third touch in an England shirt. He would assume the captaincy from Rooney two years later, when Gareth Southgate embarked on an overhaul of the squad.

“I was talking to Michael Olise at Bayern and I was asking how old he was, and he was saying at the time he was 23 and I thought, ‘Jeez, I was [England] captain then’, and I looked at him and he looked so young! So I don’t think I realised in the moment how young I was to be named captain.

“I’ve always been quite mature, even from late teenage years, always led by example, always done the right things. It felt quite natural for me. I’ve been lucky enough to do it for a long time now, and honestly the feeling of being captain still feels as good as that first moment I wore [the armband].”

Eleven years and 125 games after his England debut, Shilton will present Kane with a special cap to commemorate the achievement. It will be a busy pre-match, with Kane also expected to find time to parade the Ballon d’Or to the Wembley crowd.

Even in Kane’s world, it has been an extraordinary, whirlwind few weeks.

“I think I struggle to take it all in to be honest,” he says. “I think it is just my natural mindset to look ahead. The fact that I had just equalled the record [last month], it was, ‘right, next camp, let’s go and break the record’. Maybe tomorrow will feel a little different, actually breaking the record and being the one that sits alone on top.

“But in this period especially when there are so many games, I don’t think I’ve taken it all in. What’s happened in the last few weeks, I don’t think I’ve accepted it all, I guess. But maybe during the winter break when I’m away somewhere, on the beach, it’ll be a moment to reflect and then really soak it all in.”

#1083. Man City look to be crumbling after guilty verdict

Manchester City’s feud with the Premier League following the guilty verdict will dominate their season, but it is now events on the pitch that are proving a genuine concern.

Enzo Maresca has lost three league games in a row and, at the City Ground, there was further evidence of defensive instability, strange team selection and key players underperforming.

Eight games without a clean sheet underlines their vulnerability and Maresca has much to ponder over the international break with his team six points behind leaders Arsenal.

What a response from Nottingham Forest to Oliver Glasner’s brutal “no-compromises” rant last weekend, as the home team secured only the second league win in front of their own supporters this year.

It was a former City player, Liam Delap, who tormented them with two brilliant individual goals to give Glasner what he hopes will finally be lift-off.

"The day that Delap ARRIVES" 🤩 Nottingham Forest regain their two-goal lead! https://t.co/5yk5eIhPhe

While Forest will hope this proves a turning point in their season, these are certainly worrying times for City.

Marc Guéhi and Josko Gvardiol are both badly out of form and were replaced at half-time with injuries, while it was another alarming evening for goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

Elsewhere this afternoon, Martin Odegaard has broken the deadlock at the Emirates to give Arsenal a 1-0 lead over Hull City.

Victory would take Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of City at the top of the table before this evening’s contest at the City Ground.

Erling Haaland will be hoping for his 10th league goal in 10 games this term, having bagged nine from nine so far.

Last week’s 1-0 defeat against Brighton was the first league game he failed to score in since the opening match of the season against Bournemouth.

The Norwegian is once again leading the way in the Premier League’s scoring charts, with three goals more than his nearest rivals.

Oliver Glasner pressed the nuclear button last weekend and the big question today is how his Forest players respond.

After the 2-0 defeat at Brentford, Glasner warned there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

This usually goes one of two ways and Glasner will be hoping it produces a positive reaction.

Training has apparently been excellent this week but it will mean little unless they transfer it into a match situation.

James McAtee has been Forest’s best player so far this season and faces the club he joined as an 11 year old.

Enzo Maresca made a flawless start at Manchester City but is now enduring a stumble.

Elliot Anderson returns for the first time since his £116m move from Forest in the summer and what a signing he already appears.

Forest are already wondering whether their asking price should have been higher and, as daft as it sounds, City have probably got a bargain.

Dejan Kulusevski has opened up about the knee injury that kept him on the sidelines for over 18 months and revealed that he turned down a possible knee transplant treatment.

Kulusevski also explained how his recovery weighed heavily on his mind amid fears that he would never play football again.

The 26-year-old missed 526 days of playing time including the entirety of the 2025/26 season after suffering a patella injury during a defeat to Crystal Palace in May 2025.

He also missed the start of the current season but has since returned to action in substitute appearances against Coventry, Palace and Leeds United.

Speaking of his injury and the extent of his recovery, Kulusevski explored how he thought “it’s over, it’s over” when attempting to get back on the pitch and reignite his career before confessing to his mother that his treatment options may not work out.

Now the forward is back and fit enough to feature on a professional level and has been selected for Sweden’s Nations League games this month. Getting on the pitch against Bosnia and Herzegovina or Poland would see Kulusevski make his first international appearance in two years.

The Tottenham man also revealed why his recovery took as long as it did.

“The reason it took so long is that there are people who haven’t even recovered from injuries like this,” he told Swedish outlet Fotbollskanalen.

“I spent the whole summer talking to other doctors about having another operation. It would have been a knee transplant — swapping my knee for someone else’s.

“So I said no: ‘This is what we’ll do: if I’m in pain when I play, I’ll just have to play through the pain.’ I trained and tried to live like a normal person. I trusted that it would work out. So far, I’ve been right.”

Kulusevski went on to add that he was advised by doctors that a knee transplant had a “50/50” chance of setting his recovery back for an extended period of time.

The winger also spoke to former teammates, Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Ivan Perisic, who recommended a doctor in Serbia and Kulusevski praised the work and advise he received.

He added: “He [the doctor] was so sure it would work out. I needed someone by my side who would say to me: ‘Dejan, this is going to be fine.’ So he was important to me.”

Sweden are top of Group B4 in the Nations League and have the chance to secure promotion to League A.

#1075. AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Melissa Hobson is a freelance marine-science journalist based in Hastings, UK.

Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is working to make AI energy use more sustainable.

Artificial intelligence is exploding in popularity, and many people have concerns about the sustainability of its energy consumption. AI models need vast amounts of electricity: according to the International Energy Agency, a typical AI data centre can consume as much energy as 100,000 households each year. Energy use by US data-centre servers more than tripled between 2014 and 2023 — reaching 4.4% of the nation’s total electricity consumption. This figure is expected to at least double by 20281.

However, AI might also hold the key to improving energy efficiency: offsetting some of the demand it creates. An article published by the World Economic Forum suggests that the use of AI tools across industries — in automating tasks or monitoring real-time energy use, for example — can reduce energy consumption by up to 60%. Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes, a sustainable-development specialist and an author of the article, has been working to lower AI’s energy demands while finding ways to use the tools to reduce wider emissions.

Originally from Trinidad, Greene-Dewasmes became interested in solving energy-security issues for island states with few resources. In 2021, she completed a PhD on the green-energy transition across small island developing states at the University of York, UK, before joining the World Economic Forum in 2022. Now based in Geneva, Switzerland, Greene-Dewasmes has been the Forum’s AI and Energy Lead since 2024. Her work involves bringing together AI and energy leaders from around the world to identify shared challenges, align priorities and develop practical actions that can improve AI’s energy impact.

As well as looking at improving AI’s energy efficiency, Greene-Dewasmes and partners are exploring how models can find innovations that improve existing energy infrastructure, such as that in buildings that are already in use. Nature spoke to her about navigating the increasing energy needs of the technology and whether its benefits could outweigh this demand.

AI needs cloud networks, chips, graphics-processing units and cooling systems, all of which consume large amounts of energy. Developing and training models requires high levels of processing power to crunch the data, but AI use is much more energy intensive overall because of the scale. ChatGPT, the chatbot from technology firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, has more than 800 million users each month and receives more than 2.5 billion queries daily. As AI becomes mainstream, we need to build more energy infrastructure to keep up with the surge in demand.

But, when it comes to scaling up AI, I think the conversation is too skewed towards the energy needed to power centralized infrastructure, when there are lots of other things that will contribute to AI’s energy requirements. Large data centres will exist in only the few countries that have the money, space and resources to host them. For most of the world, AI infrastructure will be disaggregated and decentralized. For example, if one million people are using their phones more intensively because of AI, that affects the energy infrastructure.

Although more complex LLM queries are currently directed to remote data centres, some smaller tasks can be completed directly on new devices that have AI chips. As this becomes more common, what will that mean for infrastructure planning for energy? It’s much harder to measure this than the outputs from one data centre.

AI’s electricity impact is currently about 0.49% of total global electricity use — so it’s still fairly small, although it’s growing. The World Economic Forum, in collaboration with other specialists, has created a Net-Positive AI Energy Framework. It looks at how we can design AI models and infrastructure for efficiency — by optimizing chips, data-centre locations and liquid cooling, in which fluids are used for cooling owing to their high heat capacity — while using AI to bring down energy usage in high-impact sectors, such as transportation and urbanization, both by improving the efficiency of systems and coming up with solutions to global challenges.

For example, in Azerbaijan, operations that keep buildings running, including lighting, heating and cooling, account for a large proportion of the country’s carbon emissions. The Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution Azerbaijan (a public legal entity) is using AI-powered solutions to improve efficiencies as part of its nationally determined contribution commitments — the country’s pledge to reduce emissions. This includes AI solutions that adjust heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) on the basis of building occupancy and use trends, and that predict the need for maintenance before faults arise. In some cases, this use of AI to hone efficiency has brought down HVAC energy use by 25% and emissions by up to 40%.

We’re also encouraging people to use AI wisely. We want AI to reduce energy consumption overall, rather than adding strain to systems.

The aim is to gather insights from leading voices in the AI ecosystem to generate thought leadership and encourage cross-discipline learning so people aren’t working in silos. It started off as one-on-one conversations with professionals working with AI, centred on the technology’s biggest challenges and opportunities. We convened a community of about 40 people, which has increased to around 70 in nine industries around the world and is still growing. We try to hear from lots of voices: university academics, public-sector entities and technology, AI and energy companies (including renewables and nuclear) are all involved. Together with our partners, we turn these insights into guidance and frameworks that can support the wider industry.

We’ve published two reports based on the learnings gleaned from these thought leaders. Artificial Intelligence Energy Paradox explores how to balance the challenges and opportunities of AI and energy. The Net-Positive AI Energy Framework is our North Star for clean, efficient and equitable AI. We’re now working on an AI Energy Readiness Compass: a methodology to support responsible AI energy developments and identify the causes of upcoming bottlenecks in the power grid that could be problematic for AI energy use.

One particular success from these collaborations is the willingness of hyperscalers — large organizations that operate cloud computing services and data centres — to embrace grid flexibility. At first, they were reluctant to adjust when they draw power because they wanted continuous access to reliable electricity, but they have come to see the benefits of balancing demand on the grid. As a result, they have embraced power flexibility, and 18 partners supported the launch of the AI Energy Management Alliance: a coalition of companies that promotes dynamic load-shifting (changing when energy is used to align with grid loads, the availability of green energy and the best pricing).

#1073. USA pull out of U17 World Cup in Qatar over safety concerns

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The US has withdrawn from the tournament due to the risk of armed conflict in the region

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The USA have withdrawn from the Under-17 World Cup in Qatar, which begins in just over a week, citing the risk of conflict in the region.

A letter sent to players from the US Soccer Federation explaining the decision referred to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar.

It issued a level three travel advisory last month, a day after Yemen’s Houthi rebels carried out deadly airstrikes on Riyadh’s international airport, warning Americans not to travel to Qatar due to the “risk of armed conflict” and the “potential [for hostilities] to escalate beyond” areas which had already been attacked.

US Soccer’s letter to players reads: “Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament. The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

Fifa’s regulations for U17 World Cups state that nations who qualify must take part or be fined around $24,000 for withdrawing within 30 days of the tournament’s start date.

The USA reached the last 32 in the 2025 edition of the U17 World Cup, the first of five intended to be held annually in Qatar.

It had been set to play Group J games against Montenegro, Chile and Algeria. The tournament begins on 19 November and runs until 13 December.

While the tournament is going ahead several other major sporting events slated to take place in the Middle East have been cancelled or postponed due to the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis and the war between the US, Israel and Iran.

Riyadh’s Six Kings Slam, a lucrative tennis exhibition tournament, has been postponed from October to December; the Dakar Rally, also planned to take place in Saudi Arabia in January, will be moved elsewhere; Golf’s Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International event; the World Rally Championship will not longer visit Saudi Arabia and the cycling Urban World Championships were cancelled.

F1 is pressing ahead with its season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi but the 2027 Asian Cup, the continental football championship, which had been due to take place in Saudi Arabia in January next year has been postponed by nearly a year.
