#1072. Next Man United manager: Who could replace Michael Carrick?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Carrick is on the brink after another chaotic performance in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, which leaves United stuck in the bottom three during the international break

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick has been sacked by Manchester United, with the club inside the relegation zone during the international break and considering a fourth permanent manager in three years since minority owners Ineos, under Sir Jim Ratcliffe, took control of football operations.

Carrick – who impressed during his interim spell in charge last season – saw the goodwill this season evaporate after United’s worst start to a season in 40 years, with a disastrous defensive performance seeing them go two goals down against Aston Villa before a miraculous late comeback earned a 4-4 draw.

Liverpool away after the international break offers little hope of escaping the drop zone, before a trip to Lisbon in the Champions League.

While the problems United face run far deeper than the head coach – as highlighted by defender Lisandro Martinez after the defeat to Atletico Madrid earlier this month – while criticism of Carrick’s tactics came from United captain Bruno Fernandes, who has not been able to inspire the team in the manner that saw him pick up the PFA Player of the Year award and the league’s assist record last term.

So who could be in charge at Anfield and beyond in a bid to, firstly, guide the club away from a relegation battle?

The current odds-on favourite after emerging as a key target, yet Man United could face a problem getting the Argentine out of his United States contract, having committed to terms up to the next World Cup in 2030. Compensation in excess of £7m could follow, yet United are in a desperate situation and the experience and presence of Pochettino could spark a reaction from a group desperately short of inspiration. Pochettino’s powers have waned since his famous spell with Spurs, though his exit at Chelsea came at the end of a promising run to conclude the 2023/24 season. There was immense potential and excitement to start the 2026 World Cup, but a combination of the Folarin Balogun scandal and then a thumping at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 took the shine off Pochettino’s performance from the dugout. Now, it remains to be seen if he can deliver once more in club football in what would surely be his most difficult job to date.

The Englishman is available after his shock decision to leave Newcastle United in the summer. Howe told the club he needed a break from management but the chance to take charge at Old Trafford, three months later, would surely be too good to turn down if an offer arrives. The 48-year-old remains highly regarded in English football after taking over a Newcastle side in the relegation zone and leading them to the club’s highest Premier League finish in two decades, as well as their first domestic silverware in 70 years. Howe twice took Newcastle into the Champions League playing an energetic, high-intensity style of football that would be popular at Old Trafford.

Brighton have been the surprise package in the Premier League this season and the 33-year-old Hurzeler has drawn praise for turning the Seagulls into a side capable of competing with the country’s biggest clubs. Brighton’s 3-0 victory over champions Arsenal earlier this season was a masterclass in modern coaching while Hurzeler’s side also knocked United out of the Carabao Cup with a brilliant 3-2 win at Old Trafford. The Independent’s Chief Football Writer Miguel Delaney has reported that Hurzeler is admired at Old Trafford but Brighton would demand significant compensation for the highly-rated German and United may not have the cash. At Brighton, Hurzeler has also enjoyed an environment where the club have made all the right decisions off the pitch. At United, he would arguably be walking into the opposite.

The Brighton boss said on Friday: “I’m fully focused on my job here. I’ve got no time to think about these rumours because we play every three days. I have a lot of respect for Michael Carrick and the job he has done at Manchester United the last season. He's a great human being, a great personality, and I really respect him. There's nothing more to say about that. I’m really privileged to be here. I’m part of a journey [at Brighton] and I still have this feeling when I go to bed that we are not finished with our journey... “We have built this [together] over the years. We’ve had good periods, we’ve had bad periods. To build these connections you need time. You don’t take these things for granted. It’s a people business. Making a people business out of this pressure business is something I don’t take for granted and something I won’t throw away that fast.”

The former wunderkind of German coaching was reportedly on United’s radar when they sacked Ruben Amorim at the start of the year, but as an option for the summer following the World Cup. Well, that was a bit of a disaster for the former Bayern Munich and RB Leipzig coach, as Germany were knocked out in the last-32 by Paraguay. Nagelsmann, 39, would naturally be interested in managing United and the club’s director of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, previously worked with him at Red Bull.

The Spaniard has done a superb job at Aston Villa by securing Champions League qualification and ending the club’s trophy drought with victory in the Europa League. But Aston Villa will be even more determined to keep Emery given the club are only in the early stages of their rebuild under him, having completely overhauled the spine of their team over the summer. As it is, Emery enjoys complete control over his project at Villa Park, a reality he is unlikely to find at Old Trafford, while he appears enthused by the challenge of constructing a second competitive team in the Premier League. With Emery, who is under contract until 2029, United would also need to pay Villa compensation, and that may place him above their budget.

The appeal of the combustible Italian only has grown while United have been accused of becoming too passive and pedestrian on the pitch. Conte is one of the most demanding coaches in the game and would instantly bring a level of intensity and urgency that has been lacking this season, while his CV – with Serie A titles at Juventus, Inter Milan and Napoli and a Premier League crown with Chelsea – commands respect. Conte also brought an immediate improvement when he took charge of a floundering Tottenham five years ago and led them back into the Champions League, which now has to be United’s biggest concern. So the 57-year-old offers impact, but then what? Conte has a sharp tongue and is not afraid to criticise his bosses if he feels they are failing to support him. His exit from Tottenham in March 2023 followed a stunning evisceration of the club in a now legendary press conference at Southampton. United would be playing with fire but options of Conte’s calibre are few and far between.

In a statement on Friday, Conte distanced himself from the Manchester United job while branding reports that he is in “advanced negotiations” with any club as “speculation”. He said: “Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right. I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my ‘strong personality’. These reports are unfounded, as there is currently no concrete basis for such assessments.”

The former Arsenal, Barcelona and Chelsea midfielder is developing a reputation as Europe’s brightest young coach – as his brilliant Como side demonstrated by thrashing United in the Champions League on Wednesday night. The Spaniard appears committed to his project in northern Italy, though, and also has a financial incentive to continue leading Como in their debut Champions League campaign due to owning a stake in the Serie A club. The 39-year-old’s own stock is also rising and the lure of returning to one of his former clubs in the future, such as Barcelona, could result in Fabregas taking a patient and considered approach to his next move.

Well, we’ve been here before. It was Under-18s manager Darren Fletcher, who oversaw the draw with Burnley and FA Cup third-round defeat to Brighton, before Michael Carrick stepped into the breach in January. Before him, Ruud van Nistelrooy held the reins between Erik ten Hag’s dismissal and Amorim’s appointment and before that, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer experienced the same cycle of boom-and-bust that Carrick has gone through over the past 10 months. In short, there are numerous former United players who are available to remind an underperforming dressing room of the importance of the badge and the meaning of the shirt. It could be time for Fletcher to give Sir Alex another call.

#1071. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

Jorgen Strand Larsen thought he had the opener against Liverpool, but it was ruled out for offside! ❌ https://t.co/JkSKbtkvak

The other factor which seems likely to condemn Sage is his team’s boneheaded defensive lapses. Liverpool were awarded a debatable free-kick out wide, Quinten Timber let Mac Allister run off him too easily and he duly nodded Dominik Szoboszlai’s delivery past Dean Henderson with ease. Another header conceded.

Liverpool have taken the lead against Crystal Palace thanks to Alexis Mac Alister's header! 💥 https://t.co/kNal7qsQ35

Mac Allister, formerly of Brighton, endeared himself to the Holmesdale Road Stand with a priggish celebration. There was some blowback from the seats closest, but a more dominant sense of resignation. Someone in the adjoining block took out their phone and snapped a picture. Formerly hated rival scoring against you, rubbing it in with his celebration: truly one to show the grandkids.

Liverpool had put together little of substance until then, with Wirtz drifting through another half, Alexander Isak looking keen but flawed and Barcola spooning a promising shot into low-Earth orbit. The second half was better, but Isak looked to have wasted his best chance, a one-on-one with Henderson thumped too close to the goalkeeper.

Isak had his moment in the end, checking back to finish calmly at the end of a counter-attack against a tiring defence. Eight for the season for him and an assist for Wirtz, too, although it was hardly a pass of Molbyesque majesty.

“Happy for him,” Iraola said of Wirtz, also praising Isak’s movement for the German’s goal. “I think [Wirtz] has been very unlucky in the Premier League, a couple of goals disallowed and situations where he deserves honestly to score.”

So it was Liverpool’s blip righted here, despite all of Palace’s pressure. Alisson, who took some flak for his performance at Fenerbahce, was hard to fault. He may not have reached Eddie Nketiah’s stoppage-time penalty, but made a series of brave saves and deserved a clean sheet. For all that attacking talent, the long-serving goalkeeper still looks like one of Iraola’s most important players.

Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.

#1070. When will Mauricio Pochettino take charge of Manchester United?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino is the favourite to replace Michael Carrick as United head coach and could be in situ for the Premier League trip to Anfield

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager just three months into the new season with the club sitting 18th in the Premier League table.

The Old Trafford hierarchy pulled the trigger on Carrick’s departure on Thursday morning after three days of speculation following a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa which proved to be Carrick’s final match in charge.

Thoughts now turn to Carrick’s replacement with former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain manager Mauricio Pochettino the odds on favourite to take over.

Pochettino is the current manager of the United States Men’s National Team (USMNT) but has reportedly reached a verbal agreement with Man United to sign of as their new head coach. Should his appointment be confirmed when will Pochettino officially begin his tenure?

Man United’s next match comes on Sunday 22 November when they travel to Anfield to take on Liverpool. It will arguably be the most difficult start possible for whoever takes over and it is a game United need to take something from or else they risk dropping further into the relegation zone.

The current international break would usually provide a new manager with time to train and see the squad in action but Pochettino, should he be given the job, is unlikely to have such a luxury.

That is because the United States have two Nations League matches to play on November 14 and 18 during this window and Pochettino is likely to oversee both fixtures.

The Argentine is still contracted to US Soccer until the 2030 World Cup though an early departure from his deal feels increasingly likely. United have made contact with US Soccer over paying compensation to release Pochettino with rumoured figures reaching as high a $10m (£7.4m).

Should an agreement be made, Pochettino could, in theory, leave the US before the scheduled games against Haiti in order to spend time with Man United’s squad ahead of the crucial clash at Anfield.

In that case he could arrive at Carrington either the same day or a day after being formally announced as the new head coach. That would give him a maximum of nine days to prepare the team if his appointment is confirmed today (Thursday 12 November).

The more likelier option is that Pochettino leads the USMNT for their two fixtures with Haiti and reports to Carrington shortly afterwards.

In that case, he could be in post at Man United as early as Wednesday 18 November though given the time difference between the US and the UK, Pochettino would arrive late in the afternoon or early evening.

Even so, that would give him three full days, Thursday 19, Friday 20 and Saturday 21 to settle into his new environment and have time on the grass with the squad.

Whether three days will be enough for the Argentine to inspire a new manager bounce out of United’s playing group remains to be seen.

#1069. Michael Carrick sacked by Man United with club stuck in relegation zone after latest crisis

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

United have failed to win in eight Premier League games and will spend the international break 18th in the table

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager with the club sitting in the Premier League relegation places after 10 games.

A second Old Trafford comeback of the week, this time battling from two goals down twice to rescue a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday, could not save Carrick’s job and he departs United just three months into the start of the season and with his side 18th during the international break.

United ended a nine-game winless run when they came from two goals down to beat Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday but they have not won in eight attempts in the Premier League and have just one top-flight win this campaign.

It represents a stark turnaround from Carrick’s positive impact as interim manager last season, when the former midfielder went beyond expectations after replacing Ruben Amorim in January, steadying the ship and guiding them to Champions League qualification.

Carrick’s position has been under threat since the damaging defeats against Como and Bournemouth last month, but he survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy and was given time to turn results around, but speculation over a change begun the day after Sunday’s chaotic draw and United States boss Mauricio Pochettino is expected to succeed Carrick having reportedly reached a verbal agreement with the club.

United have made contact with US Soccer over compensation for Pochettino with a reported figure of $10m (£7.4m) set to be paid to release him from his contract which was due to run through to the 2030 World Cup. His current staff are set to join him at Old Trafford and would require further compensation payments.

The timing of the November international break, with a full two weeks before their next game away to Liverpool in the Premier League, has prompted United to finally act and leave minority owners Ineos searching for a fourth permanent manager in three years.

Though Pochettino is the overwhelming favourite to become the next head coach, Eddie Howe is available following his departure from Newcastle in the summer while former Bayern Munich and Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann is also an option. Aston Villa’s Unai Emery and Brighton’s Fabian Hurzeler are admired but their clubs would demand significant compensation.

Manchester United confirmed the news of Carrick’s exit with a statement which reads: “Manchester United can confirm that Michael Carrick has departed his role as men’s first-team head coach.

“Michael rejoined the club in January and guided the team to a third-placed Premier League finish by winning 12 out of the remaining 17 games of the 2025/26 season, accumulating the highest points tally in the league during that period.

“After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions.

“Michael is, and always will be, a Manchester United legend. Just as he did as a player, he has conducted himself with the highest standards of dedication and professionalism throughout his time back with the club. His leadership and achievements last season will always be fondly remembered.

“The club intends to appoint a permanent successor as quickly as possible.”

Carrick initially returned to Old Trafford as interim manager – his second stint in caretaker role – after the dismissal of Amorim at the beginning of the year. He was rewarded with the full-time position after guiding United to third in the Premier League last term and securing a return to the Champions League.

United spent £155m on three new midfielders this summer – signing Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andre Santos, after missing out on their top targets Elliott Anderson and Sandro Tonali – but failed to sign a back-up left-back to Luke Shaw or another forward to support the injury-prone Benjamin Sesko.

But defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club’s hierarchy for not doing more to support Carrick following the 2-1 defeat to Atletico Madrid earlier this month while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned his manager’s tactics following the 4-1 loss at Como a week later.

Carrick had gambled by dropping captain Fernandes for the home match against Bournemouth but a dismal 3-0 defeat instead highlighted how a fractured dressing room has unravelled since the beginning of the season.

Carrick said Fernandes did not play against Bournemouth due to “pure football” reasons before holding clear-the-air talks with the Portuguese and selecting him to start as his captain in the game at Stamford Bridge.

Another defeat followed against Chelsea before United finally ended their losing run by beating Roma. The stirring win did not save Carrick’s job, however, even after another remarkable comeback against Aston Villa on Sunday.

United have conceded 30 goals in their 14 games this season and have won just three times – against newly promoted Ipswich in the Premier League and Sabah and Roma in Europe. They will travel to Liverpool on 22 November having spent the fortnight in the bottom three.

#1068. New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: Blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

For decades, scientists thought of the blood–brain barrier as an impenetrable layer. Overtime that view has changed, as researchers realized the barrier was more permeable than first thought. Now a team have catalogued almost 100 proteins that can pass through it to maintain brain health.1

The team also found that the transport of some of these crucial proteins breaks down in mice with brain disease that mimic early-stage Alzheimer’s disease.

“The paradigm in the field has been that the blood–brain barrier is normally impermeable and then becomes leaky as a result of Alzheimer’s disease,” says study co-author Andrew Yang, a neuroscientist at Gladstone Institute of Neurological Disease in San Francisco, California. Instead, his team’s work suggests that the blood–brain barrier actively imports proteins that the brain needs to function and the loss of these proteins drives the dysfunction seen early in the disease, he adds.

Yang and his colleagues developed a technique to label a large array of proteins in the blood and track those that can enter the brain. Of the 861 proteins they mapped, 92 crossed the blood–brain barrier into the brain. Most of these proteins were produced in distant organs, particularly the liver.

The team focused on apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) which has been linked to potential protective effects against Alzheimer’s disease. Once inside the brain, APOA1 stimulates brain cells called astrocytes to release cholesterol, which is important for maintaining the synapses through which neurons communicate. But how the protein crossed the blood-brain barrier has been unclear until now, says Yang.

His team found that two receptors for APOA1 — SR-B1 and ABCA1 — are present on the blood–brain barrier as well as astrocytes. This suggests how the protein moves from the blood-brain barrier to the specific brain cells that need them, the authors say.

When Yang’s team blocked the ABCA1 receptor in laboratory-grown astrocytes, the protein no longer had the same cholesterol-regulating effects.

Scientists have long known that the blood–brain barrier breaks down as Alzheimer’s advances, letting harmful molecules leak into the brain. Yang’s team found that a different problem emerges first.

Using their labelling technique in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease, the researchers found that the blood–brain barrier stopped importing protective proteins such as APOA1 into the brain before the barrier began to break down. This disruption to the protein transport was accompanied by a loss of neuronal connections, behavioural changes and other early hallmarks of the disease.

Yang and the team wondered whether increasing the supply of APOA1 in the blood might help to counter some of the damage caused by Alzheimer’s disease. To find out, the team engineered mice with Alzheimer’s to produce extra APOA1 in the liver. When more APOA1 crossed their blood–brain barrier and entered the brain, the mice showed fewer Alzheimer’s-disease-related markers. For example, they had reduced fat build-up in astrocytes and lower levels of inflammatory molecules.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2

Zhou, H. et al. Cell https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.039 (2026).

#1067. Football fan arrest numbers branded ‘unacceptable’ by policing chief

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Police praised supporters who travelled to North America for their conduct but warned that wider football-related disorder remains a concern

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Latest arrest figures for fans watching last summer’s World Cup are "unacceptably" high despite excluding linked crimes such as domestic abuse, football’s policing lead has said.

Home Office data shows 357 arrests occurred in England and Wales linked to fans watching England matches during the North American tournament, compared to just 19 arrests at the event itself.

Chief Constable Mark Hobrough, National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) lead for football policing, praised travelling fans for "exemplary" behaviour, but described conduct at home during the World Cup and 2025-26 domestic season as far more troubling.

He said: "Though the vast majority of supporters attending domestic fixtures in the UK are law-abiding and enjoy supporting their teams at great games, there still remain an unacceptable number who spoil the event for others.

"2,025 people were arrested for football-related incidents during the domestic season in 2025-26, and disappointingly this number is up from 2,004 in 2024-25.

"In addition, 357 people were arrested in England and Wales for football-related incidents during the 2026 World Cup alone.

"Sadly, these figures do not paint a full picture as they do not include many of the associated offences, such as domestic abuse, which often occur behind closed doors after the full-time whistle has blown and in many cases nowhere near any stadium or club with individuals who’ve not attended any game themselves.

"However, as the figures show, we are continuing to take action against those responsible, and moving forward, we will continue to work with our partners including the Crown Prosecution Service, the Premier League, the EFL and the Football Association to collectively make football a safe environment for the overwhelming majority of supporters who just want to enjoy the game."

Home Office figures for 2025-26, first released in July showing 1,963 football-related arrests or police actions, have now been revised to 2,025.

Total arrests across the 2025-26 season—including domestic games, the World Cup, and European fixtures abroad—reached 2,403, falling from 2,584 in 2023-24, the previous men’s tournament season.

Tournament-related arrests within England and Wales increased compared to 2023-24, a change the Home Office attributed to better recording and awareness among police forces.

The American trained with the Seasiders in 2014

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After being dubbed the ‘new Pele’ at the tender age of 14, Freddy Adu’s career would end up taking him to some unexpected places.

After becoming the youngest-ever player to appear in United States professional sports when he made his D.C. United debut in 2004, Adu had stints playing in Portugal, France, Greece, Turkey and Brazil over the next decade.

After a stint with Salvador-based Brazilian side Bahia ended, Adu’s next opportunity came at Blackpool, with the then-Championship side taking the American on trial in February 2014.

And while moving from the Brazilian summer to a Blackpool winter would be a culture shock to most, Adu looks back at his time with the Seasiders fondly.

“I had a good time there, it was great!” he tells FourFourTwo. “I was a free agent after Brazil, and Blackpool was cool!”

“I liked it there, I remember I really did enjoy my time there, being around those guys, but the football was really different, compared to what I was used to.”

Adu’s nomadic career to this point had seen him adapt to plenty of new surroundings, but he admits that the rough-and-tumble style of a second-tier English side was something new to him.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“It was more direct and very physically demanding, so my style of play didn’t exactly mesh with the team,” he admits.

Blackpool would decide against offering Adu a contract, but would allow him to continue training with the club as Adu looked for his next opportunity.

After stints training in Norway and the Netherlands, he would sign with Serbian side FK Jagodina in July 2014, in a move that again didn’t work out for him.

“I went to Serbia and just played the one game, I was only there for about six months,” Adu continues. “At that point in my career, I just needed to try to get somewhere, get some playing time and get my love for soccer back again. It didn’t end up happening over there, I wasn’t happy there.

“They sell you this story but you get there and things are completely different, so I was just trying to bide my time and get out of there.

"Hindsight isn’t 20/20, but there are a lot of decisions I would have made differently, as far as teams go, if I had that opportunity.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1065. Man United Supporters’ Trust underlines ‘depressing moment’ after Michael Carrick sacked

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The supporters’ group said “responsibility for United’s problems... lie with the ownership” rather than Carrick

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) has branded Michael Carrick’s sacking “another depressing moment” and argued the club’s problems rest primarily with its ownership, in a now-familiar plea to end the ongoing feeling of crisis at Old Trafford.

United sacked Carrick just 10 games into the Premier League season with the club in the relegation zone and having won just once in this domestic campaign.

The club’s hierarchy met minority owner Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick’s future and a statement on Thursday said that it had “come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions”.

Former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino, who currently manages the US men’s national team, is in line to replace him.

The club statement paid tribute to former midfielder Carrick as a “Manchester United legend” and the MUST statement concurred, saying “his standing among supporters remains undiminished”, but criticised the ownership for the spiral the club has found itself in.

It said: “Michael Carrick’s departure marks another depressing moment for Manchester United. We thank him for his service and for restoring hope during the second half of last season. His standing among supporters remains undiminished.

“The reason Manchester United fans have continued to support Michael Carrick in recent weeks is that they know that responsibility for United’s problems do not primarily rest with him or indeed his predecessors as manager. They lie with the ownership.

“The Glazers’ debt-funded takeover continues to burden the club. When Ineos came in they promised sporting excellence, but yet with repeated changes in football leadership we have seen anything but.

“It is time for the owners to explain themselves and show some accountability.”

MUST continued to criticise “aggressive ticketing policies” which “have further damaged relations with supporters”, arguing “supporters are being asked to pay the price for the owners’ mismanagement as well as their stadium ambitions through higher charges and diminished rights”.

It continued: “The unprecedented scale of the booing at Old Trafford, alongside public criticism from senior players in recent weeks, now points to a deeper deterioration. These are signs of a club becoming more divided, with the bond between supporters, players and those running Manchester United under increasing strain.”

Defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club’s hierarchy for not doing more to support Carrick in the transfer market following the 2-1 Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid last month, while dire on-pitch performances have resulted in protests against the ownership and loud booing of the players, although there were public displays of support for Carrick by fans at Old Trafford.

MUST concluded: “The owners must allow senior club management to change direction: show accountability, rebuild trust, listen to supporters and recognise that their loyalty is fundamental to football success.

“Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”

#1062. Destiny brought Mauricio Pochettino to Man United - but one huge question remains

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Argentine has come close to becoming Manchester United manager on three separate prior occasions. Now the stars appear to have finally aligned, but is it too late for either the man or the club?

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

On Sunday evening, Mauricio Pochettino got the call he had been waiting for.

He and long-time assistant Jesus Perez had frequently asked about Manchester United over the last decade. They would often contact friends in the game who were connected to Old Trafford, looking to find out what was happening, whether there could be an opening.

Pochettino came very close to taking one of those openings on at least three occasions: 2018, 2021 and 2024. Now, elements might finally have aligned.

It is a call that others at Old Trafford have long waited for, too. Back when they had a much publicised dinner in 2016, Sir Alex Ferguson essentially told Pochettino he should be the United manager. The Argentine was enthralled at that meeting by stories from one of the game’s great glory eras, and a sense of magic he had felt just standing in Old Trafford had been deepened.

Pochettino had been especially taken by Ferguson’s account of rebuilding United from the 1980s, initially drawing comparisons with what he was doing at Tottenham Hotspur. Now, he’s set to take on that exact same job, if one that has become so much bigger than in 2016. It is arguably even bigger than in 1986.

Pochettino, however, is fired by the idea of being the man to finally fix United. It has become one of the great managerial quests. The United hierarchy have ultimately gone for him because of that personality, and his standing. They don’t want a coach who hasn’t worked at this level. They want someone ready. Both the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe can sense that, since the two sides of the United ownership have known Pochettino for years.

If this is an appointment that always felt destined, though, that does raise one big question. Is this the right moment for it? Is it like Jose Mourinho, in that it came too late? Is it typical of modern United in that sense? Is it the same old “magical thinking” of hoping a famous name saves them, when the game has changed and the actual problems are now so structural?

Pochettino probably should have gone to United in 2016 or 2018, when he was at a peak in terms of being one of the most exciting coaches in football. The club did consider a move in the summer of 2016, but sources say an exit clause was allowed to expire. How different things could have been.

Old Trafford insiders are now talking about the value of “a name”, but the hierarchy did pass on Pochettino in 2024, when they initially considered sacking Erik ten Hag before ultimately deciding to stick with the Dutchman. His interview wasn’t seen as convincing as that of Thomas Tuchel or Roberto De Zerbi. Those who know him also say he is closer to being “a manager” now, in terms of a wider outlook, rather than the on-the-grass coach that so drove Spurs.

The very fact United are negotiating to pry him from the United States national team, without wishing to be disrespectful, also illustrates how his stock has recently dropped. Some close to Pochettino would nevertheless put that down to necessary choices at certain moments. Taking charge of the hosts of the biggest World Cup ever, that had so much pomp around it, was too enticing. Before that, he probably should have pushed to go to United or Real Madrid in 2018 but he was convinced he could do something special with Spurs. He’d put too much into it.

And that does point to one of the other great twists of fate in modern football, where Pochettino’s profile could be completely different. His Tottenham team were genuinely one of the best in Europe over 2016-18, and one of the great Premier League teams. To achieve 86 points in 2016-17, on what was then only the sixth highest wage bill in English football, was genuine alchemy. It was immense overperformance, fostered by a side that could just overrun you.

We also now know that the wage bill of the eventual champions for that season, Chelsea, had in part come from signings that had been secured by payments against the rules. The punishment from that guilty verdict still looks weak. There is a strong argument that Chelsea should have been stripped of the 2015 and 2017 titles. Pochettino himself said as much in a wide-ranging interview with The Independent and other media in September: “I’ve said that, that we should win one title, one Premier League. We should have been awarded it… for sure, we deserve to be champions for that year.”

Had that justice been done, Pochettino would not just be a “name” who created an exciting Spurs once. He would be an English champion, and one responsible for one of the most historic titles given the much wealthier competition. A great institution would have won just their third title, and first in 56 years.

Both he and Spurs could have had their futures transformed, as well as their place in history. It would have been a modern equivalent of what Ferguson himself did with Aberdeen.

Now, he wants to follow Ferguson in a different way. This is the job he has been waiting for.

A certain apathy towards the US job was displayed in that September interview when he spoke about how his contract didn’t necessarily mean he’d stay the full term.

For all of that, and how their World Cup campaign ended in the chaos of Donald Trump’s disruptive interference in the Falorin Balogun case, there were very impressive spells when the US really looked like a classic Pochettino team. The way they ripped into Paraguay was reminiscent of Spurs 2016-18, right up to some of the flourishes. And that was in a much more limited and restricted environment than a club team.

This is the other thing about just taking the job, too. Regardless of United’s current problems, and perceptions of where Pochettino is in his career, he is energised by this. He has that bite. As one figure who knows him well says, “he has got the IP, he has got the brand, he has got the experience”.

Having already worked for Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain, he’s been at big clubs with demanding owners. He has the mettle for that. And he now looks set to have the big job he’s always wanted.

#1060. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. The west Londoners are again dominating possession in and near the hinterland of the Sunderland box, but it’s all a bit after you Claude and ultimately Roefs gladly picks up an anaemic cross. Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Palmer pulls back for Gusto whose dinky, cheeky chip tries to find Roefs off his line. He doesn’t succeed and the Dutch goalkeeper claims with ease.

Rogers tries to find Palmer, but the ball is too long and Roefs gobbles up with ease.

Meanwhile, Hume looks injured and Chelsea do not give the ball back after Sunderland kicked it off. You won’t be shocked to hear that the home fans are not happy with that...

Change for Sunderland, Brobbey off for Isador. The Dutchman has been brilliant today, he might have scored a couple of goals, but despite not finding the back of the net he has proved a handful for the Chelsea backline. I would have kept him on for longer...

Chelsea looking better this half, they’re seeing plenty of the ball but have not had a shot on goal since the break. In fact there have only been two touches in either box this 45...Sunderland won’t mind that at 1-0.

Chelsea haven’t been able to play through Sunderland and you think they’d need to bring on a physical presence up front if that’s to change.

Another chance for Sunderland - they break down the right before Hume sends in a low ball to the penalty box, it’s met first time by Le Fee, I think, and Penders saves low to his right. Pressure from Sunderland. A good bit of possession ends with Mukiele swinging in a lovely cross from the right which Chelsea are forced to head clear for a corner. Rogers picks up the ball in the middle just inside the Sunderland half and is immediately pick-pocketed by one of three Sunderland players. The Chelsea men have not been allowed to settle when they have a sniff of a mini counter.

Good, feisty opening to this half, Chelsea look more up for it, though to be fair they couldn’t look any more insipid than they did in the first 45. Meanwhile, Brobbey shoves Lavia and earns a yellow. Think that’s three yellows for the hosts now.

It is going to be fascinating to see how a team with well known - and long standing - disciplinary issues copes with a pressurised pursuit of an equaliser. Watch it unfold with interest.

Brobbey lays the ball off for Meunier in the final third, it’s asking a lot of the Belgian but his compounds the Dutchman’s error with one of his own - stretching for the ball and taking out Caicedo. Something for which he earns a needless yellow card.

There’s a bit of argy bargy on the pitch, not sure what started that but the referee Jarred Gillett has to have a word with several players. All a bit of handbags really.

They’re back under way on the banks of the Wear. Chelsea have been insipid and you imagine they won’t be as bed these next 45 minutes. Can Sunderland play with the same aggression and energy? We’re about to find out.

Changes Estevao on for Colwill, interesting substitution to say the least...

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The half ends with an audacious attempt at goal from Rogers, a full 40 yards out from a free kick. It’s catching practice for Roefs and that sums up Chelsea as an attacking force in the first 45. Sunderland are well worth their lead.

Rogers has a shot-cum-cross from the left and it sails high, wide and not so handsome. He’s been on the periphery this half, as has Palmer and that explains as much as anything why they are behind. Sunderland have cut out the supply to him and Roefs has had little to do as a result.

Approaching half-time and save for the contentious VAR call when he wanted a penalty, Cole Palmer has done absolutely nothing. Brobbey wants the ball at every opportunity and Sunderland would be well advised to give it to him. Colwill is has his hands full.

Another chance for Sunderland as Brobbey bullies Colwill on the halfway line before driving at Fofana. He gets to the edge of the area, beats the Chelsea defender before his shot goes wide. The last touch took him too wide, but again, promising signs for the hosts.

Sunderland are being aggressive, they need to be and it’s a contrast from the previous month. With that approach, however, comes risks and Mukiele gives away a free-kick inside his own half. Luckily for him, nothing comes from the set-piece.

First chance of the game for Chelsea and, as with Brobbey 10 minutes ago, it should have found the back of the net. Rogers is the culprit - he sends his header wide of the right post after a grade-A cross from Palestra.

One-all in terms of great chances...but the score remains 0-0.

Palmer is bundled over on the outskirts of the area and he and Chelsea players appeal for something - could be a free-kick of penalty...the referee is having nothing of it. Yellow card for Ahoka for a foul on Caicado, he may need to walk a tightrope for the rest of the match. But it’s an illustration of the energy and purpose with which Sunderland have approached this match.

Another good chance for Sunderland and once again Talbi proves his worth. He cuts back onto his right and delivers a peach of a cross from the left. This is a big afternoon for both teams. It will be an emotional one, too, for Jordan Henderson, who started his career at Sunderland many years ago. Xabi Alonso has confirmed he has been picked because of the quality he provides, rather than any sentimental value, and Regis Le Bris revealed ahead of the fixture he tried to bring the England international home during the summer window, when Chelsea attempted to sign Granit Xhaka.

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” said Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

“I thought that it could have been a good signing for the club, a good symbol, a great player, a great leader. But the market is the market.”

“We have to stay consistent and true to our identity. It’s always difficult to predict what the other side does but you have to focus on yourself and connect with the fans and impose our ideas.”

“He’s loved by fans and team, so we know the situation at beginning of season. He is an important player for us and didn’t start for various reasons, but has qualities run in behind and finish - he’s excited worked and has worked hard.”

I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

In the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Here’s Matt Law’s article on Why Chelsea have gone from pint-sized players to taller trees...

Those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

Your Chelsea side today! ✔️ #CFC | #SUNCHE https://t.co/ciaILJeAuu

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1058. Michael Carrick sacked LIVE: Man Utd part ways with manager and move to complete Pochettino deal

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The former United midfielder was let go today after the club’s worst start to a domestic season in 40 years

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United manager after overseeing the club’s worst start to the Premier League season in 40 years, with Mauricio Pochettino looking set to replace him.

A second Old Trafford comeback of the week, this time battling from two goals down twice to rescue a 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday, was not enough to save Carrick’s job and the club announced on Thursday that it had parted ways with him after just 10 games of the season and with his side 18th during the international break.

United ended a nine-game winless run when they came from two goals down to beat Roma in the Champions League last week but they have not won in eight attempts in the Premier League and have just one top-flight win this campaign.

Carrick survived crisis talks with the United hierarchy after defeats to Como and Bournemouth last month and was given time to turn results around, but speculation over a change begun the day after Sunday’s chaotic draw and The Independent understands contact was initially made with United States boss Pochettino over succeeding Carrick on Monday.

The Old Trafford hierarchy, including Jason Wilcox, Omar Berrarda and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, met in Monaco to discuss Carrick’s future and the club are on the verge of hashing out a deal with Pochettino, who is reportedly ready to accept the position.

Follow latest updates from Old Trafford here:

Paul Scholes thinks Man United might be going in for Mauricio Pochettino a few years too late.

He said on The Good, The Bad & The Football: “I love Pochettino and we work with him at Soccer Aid, didn’t we, he’s a he’s a great man. I think he’s got the presence to manage a big football club like Manchester United.

“He’s got the respect to do it. He works with young players which obviously Manchester United want. My only slight concern is have that we come a little bit too late to the party.

“I think we’ve done that in the past. You look at Van Gaal, his best years were probably behind him. Mourinho again, I think his best years were probably behind him. Saying that, I’m not ruling out what he’s going to do with this Real Madrid team because this Real Madrid team look good.

“I just - when you really think about when we was talking about this two or three weeks ago after the Bournemouth game I don’t think any of us mentioned Pochettino.”

The Manchester United Supporters’ Trust (MUST) has branded Michael Carrick’s sacking “another depressing moment” and argued the club’s problems rest primarily with its ownership, in a now-familiar plea to end the ongoing feeling of crisis at Old Trafford.

United sacked Carrick just 10 games into the Premier League season with the club in the relegation zone and having won just once in this domestic campaign.

The club’s hierarchy met minority owner Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco on Wednesday to discuss Carrick’s future and a statement on Thursday said that it had “come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions”.

Today is only the sixth time in Premier League history two managers - Michael Carrick and Pierre Sage - have left their positions on the same day during a season.

The last time it happened actually wasn’t that long ago, with Wolves boss Gary O'Neil and Southampton manager Russell Martin both getting canned on 15 December 2024.

Pochettino is still contracted to US Soccer until the 2030 World Cup though an early departure from his deal feels increasingly likely. United have made contact with US Soccer over paying compensation to release Pochettino with rumoured figures reaching as high a $10m (£7.4m).

Should an agreement be made, Pochettino could, in theory, leave the US before the scheduled games against Haiti in order to spend time with Man United’s squad ahead of the crucial clash at Anfield.

In that case he could arrive at Carrington either the same day or a day after being formally announced as the new head coach. That would give him a maximum of nine days to prepare the team if his appointment is confirmed today (Thursday 12 November).

The more likelier option is that Pochettino leads the USMNT for their two fixtures with Haiti and reports to Carrington shortly afterwards.

In that case, he could be in post at Man United as early as Wednesday 18 November though given the time difference between the US and the UK, Pochettino would arrive late in the afternoon or early evening.

Even so, that would give him three full days, Thursday 19, Friday 20 and Saturday 21 to settle into his new environment and have time on the grass with the squad.

Thoughts have now turned to Michael Carrick’s replacement with former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain manager Mauricio Pochettino the odds on favourite to take over.

Pochettino is the current manager of the United States Men’s National Team (USMNT) but has reportedly reached a verbal agreement with Man United to sign of as their new head coach. Should his appointment be confirmed when will Pochettino officially begin his tenure?

Man United’s next match comes on Sunday 22 November when they travel to Anfield to take on Liverpool. It will arguably be the most difficult start possible for whoever takes over and it is a game United need to take something from or else they risk dropping further into the relegation zone.

The current international break would usually provide a new manager with time to train and see the squad in action but Pochettino, should he be given the job, is unlikely to have such a luxury.

That is because the United States have two Nations League matches to play on November 14 and 18 during this window and Pochettino is likely to oversee both fixtures.

Gary Neville has branded Manchester United ‘classless’ over how they handled the dismissal of Michael Carrick.

United finally pulled the trigger on Carrick’s sacking after days of leaving their manager in limbo, despite it becoming near-common knowledge that the club had been speaking to Mauricio Pochettino in an effort to acquire him as his replacement.

Speaking on the Overlap’s Stick to Football podcast, which was recorded prior to Thursday’s confirmation, he said: “We’re sat here today recording this programme knowing that Michael Carrick is going to be sacked tomorrow, knowing that they’re speaking to Mauricio Pochettino, knowing that they’ve spoken to (Julian) Nagelsmann, (Eddie) Howe – and they should be doing that by the way, I’m not saying they shouldn’t be doing that…

“But I think the fact they’re in Monaco now and they can’t sack him today knowing that it’s happening, to me it just feels a little bit clumsy, it feels a little bit classless.

“I think if you live in Monaco, you can’t leave a guy hanging for 24 or 48 hours just because you live in Monaco, that can’t happen.”

Manchester United are closing in on a deal to appoint Mauricio Pochettino before their next game against Liverpool following Michael Carrick’s sacking.

United must strike a deal with US Soccer, with a solution required over the United States’ next two international games in particular, while the club’s hierarchy is meeting at a Monaco summit to finalise a decision over the club’s manager.

Compensation, worth an initial $7m (£5.3m), will be a formality due to the clause in Pochettino’s existing contract, that runs until the 2030 World Cup.

But one major hurdle remains to ensure Pochettino can arrive in time for the trip to Anfield.

Rio Ferdinand has shown his support for former Manchester United team-mate Michael Carrick after his sacking.

“Forever legend!” he posted on X. “Showed dignity and class as always.”

He later criticised the club’s official statement confirming his exit, posting: “Man United statement like ChatGPT... I wanna hear a voice!”

Manchester United’s penchant for implosion during the first half of the season, often after a summer of intense financial backing, is quite evident from this stat.

The club’s last five permanent managers have all been sacked between 28 October and 5 January.

It’s almost as if recruitment and management are not aligned...

Crystal Palace have sacked manager Pierre Sage after the club slumped to bottom of the Premier League table for the first time since December 2017.

The Frenchman moved to Selhurst Park on a three-year contract this summer after an impressive year at Lens, where he led the club to a runner-up finish in Ligue 1, won the Coupe de France and Trophee des Champions titles for the first time, and qualified for the Champions League.

But he was unable to replicate that success across his 16 games in all competitions at Palace, who have conceded the most goals of any top-flight side this season and claimed just seven points out of a possible 30 during his tenure, and sit two points off safety going into the November international break.

#1057. Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

A study suggests that people are being misdiagnosed as having obesity with a metric known as the body mass index (BMI).Credit: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty

Clinicians have debated for years whether body mass index (BMI) — a metric derived from a person’s height and weight — is the best way to define and diagnose obesity. Now, an approach that measures waist circumference and focuses more closely on excess body fat has proved to be better than BMI at predicting a person’s risk of death.

New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health

New obesity definition sidelines BMI to focus on health

An analysis of data collected from more than 800,000 individuals found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The study was published today in Nature1.

Physicians know that BMI — calculated by dividing a person’s weight by the square of their height — doesn’t accurately reflect body composition. For example, a muscular person might have an elevated BMI but have little body fat. The latest study “reinforces that BMI is not a good measure of obesity at the individual level and is not good in terms of predicting who is going to develop cardiometabolic disease in the long term,” says Cátia Martins, an obesity researcher at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.

But given how simple it is to calculate BMI, it remains the most widely used tool to classify obesity.

A person is usually diagnosed with obesity if they have a BMI of 30 or higher. The approach presented in the study — called the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, or CAD-obesity — goes beyond BMI, combining it with measures, such as waist circumference, that are linked to excess body fat. Physicians know that when fat tissue is preferentially stored in the abdominal area, it is associated with more negative health consequences than when it’s stored elsewhere, Martins says.

Why BMI is flawed — and how to redefine obesity

Why BMI is flawed — and how to redefine obesity

Under the CAD-obesity system2, first proposed last year, people with obesity who also have at least one of 18 specific health problems — including heart failure and sleep apnoea — are classified as having ‘clinical obesity’. This indicates that excess fat is harming their organs and tissues. Those with obesity, but without any of these health problems, are classified as having ‘preclinical obesity’, in which a person has excess fat but their organs are functioning normally.

“We did not know until now whether or not this new framework had implications in the real world and a prognostic value,” says Francesco Rubino, a weight-loss surgeon at King’s College London who led the effort to create the new system and is a co-author of the Nature paper.

But Rubino and his colleagues proved the system’s worth by examining medical records from four large groups of people in China, Spain, the United Kingdom and the United States. They used data from three of those cohorts, in which more than 50,000 deaths occurred over up to 15 years, to determine whether BMI or the new system was a better indicator of elevated mortality risk.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5

Read the related Clinical Briefing, ‘Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method’.

And listen to a related podcast that discusses this study here.

Diego Demme explains why he retired from football at 34 years of age

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For 16 years, football was Diego Demme's way of life. It took him from the lower leagues of German football to the heights of the Bundesliga and Serie A, where he helped RB Leipzig establish themselves among Europe's elite, and Napoli end a 33-year wait for the Scudetto.

But after suffering two serious head injuries in the space of four months, Demme faced a difficult choice: continue playing the sport he loved or risk jeopardising his health and his family's future. On September 23, the former Germany international announced his retirement from professional football.

"I retired because of the two head injuries I had in the last two years. That was a difficult time for me, and that’s why I decided to finish my career," Demme admitted to FourFourTwo. "I wanted to stop while I was healthy, and after the problems I had with my head injuries, I decided to not take any risk again on the field."

After developing at Arminia Bielefeld and Paderborn, Demme helped Leipzig achieve two promotions, reach the 2019 DFB-Pokal Final and become Champions League regulars, before swapping the Bundesliga leaders for a Napoli side in crisis.

Demme helped Napoli win their first trophy in six years with the 2019/20 Coppa Italia before winning the 2022/23 Scudetto. After four and a half years in Italy, he returned to Germany in 2024, initially taking on the captaincy at Hertha Berlin. However, his homecoming soon turned into a nightmare.

On September 15, 2024, Demme took a knee to the chin during Hertha's 2–0 defeat to Fortuna Düsseldorf. Although he initially continued playing, he subsequently experienced headaches, dizziness, and problems with his right eye.

Four months later, Demme was struck in the temple by a ball from close range during training, causing him to lose consciousness. The consequences lingered, with recurring headaches, dizziness, and psychological difficulties contributing to 27 missed matches across his final two seasons.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"It was a difficult situation. I felt very bad due to the concussions, and that was the first time I felt, ‘What the f**k is going on?' I couldn’t drive the car. I needed to be there for my kids, and I couldn’t. I have a wife and family, and the most important thing was to be there for them, so I felt it was better to stop football."

Despite attracting interest from Italian clubs including Empoli, Cesena, Catania and Sorrento, Demme decided against extending his playing career. Retirement, however, has hardly meant slowing down.

The 34-year-old is now running two Neapolitan pizzerias in Berlin, overseeing the construction of his house in Kleinmachnow and pursuing qualifications in padel coaching and sports massage. Above all, he is enjoying more time with his daughters, six-year-old Gia and three-year-old Ellie.

Nor has he abandoned competitive sport. Alongside training in boxing, grappling and mixed martial arts, Demme is returning to football with Plyrs United in the Icon League, the indoor small-sided competition founded by Toni Kroos and Elias Nerlich.

"I didn't want to join another club where I'd move due to the fact that my eldest daughter started school this summer, so I decided to stop. But now, I feel good again, and I feel like the old Diego before my injuries. I will play the Icon League because the physical risk isn't as much as a regular Bundesliga match."

From the Coppa Italia to the Scudetto, Demme has spent his career chasing football's greatest prizes. Now, he's found a reward that no trophy can match: the chance to grow old in good health and watch his daughters grow up.

After getting his big breakthrough as the co-founder of the football analytics website Breaking The Lines, Zachary Lowy has been able to tap into his footballing expertise for a number of esteemed outlets like ESPN, FotMob, The Times, The Independent and Urban Pitch. Since joining FourFourTwo as a freelancer in 2025, Lowy has been able to cover a wide range of topics from analyzing the sweeping changes to the MLS season to interviewing key figures like Asamoah Gyan and Rob Holding. Fluent in Spanish, Portuguese and Italian, Lowy’s versatile skillset has allowed him to traverse a number of different fields when covering major competitions like the FIFA Club World Cup. In addition to football, he is also a seasoned participant of other sports like pickleball, tennis, and volleyball.
